q: You are under way along the coast and not talking to anyone. Which channel do you keep the radio on?
a: Channel 16, the distress, safety and calling channel
o: Channel 70, so you hear the coastguard by voice
Channel 6, the intership channel for yachts
Channel 13, the channel used by all leisure craft
why: Under way, keep watch on 16 so you hear distress and safety calls and anyone calling you.

q: Your crew scrolls to channel 70 to call a friend, but the set will not let him talk there. Why?
a: Channel 70 carries only DSC digital calls, never voice
o: Channel 70 is kept for the coastguard's voice traffic
Channel 70 only works for voice on high power, 25 W
Channel 70 is for marinas and needs their permission
why: Channel 70 is reserved for DSC data; voice there would block distress alerts.

q: A ship crossing ahead calls you on 16 and asks you to go to channel 13. What is 13 for?
o: DSC alerts and calls between ships
Port operations inside the harbour
Public calls to telephones ashore
why: Channel 13 is the international bridge-to-bridge channel for navigation safety.

fig.note: The ship calls you on 16: "go to 13"

q: You want to call a yacht you met yesterday. You do not know which channel they listen to. Where do you make the first call?
a: On 16, then move to a working channel
o: On 70, then move to a working channel
On 13, then stay there to talk
On the nearest marina's channel
why: 16 is the calling channel; once in contact, both move off it.

q: Your friend answers your call on 16. Which channel do you suggest for the conversation?
a: An intership channel such as 72 or 77
o: Channel 70, because it is always quiet
Stay on 16, as the chat will be short
The marina's port operations channel
why: Yacht-to-yacht talk goes on an intership simplex channel, not 16, 70 or a port channel.

q: You and a friend want a long chat about tomorrow's route. Both 6 and 72 are free. Which do you choose?
a: 72 — keep 6 clear, as it is also used in search and rescue
o: 6 — it is the intership channel meant for chats
6 — it carries further than 72 at the same power
72 — channel 6 is only for DSC data and alerts
why: Channel 6 is also the on-scene channel for search and rescue; use 72 or 77 for social talk.

q: You and your friend both select the same duplex channel. You can hear the coast station on it, but not each other. Why?
a: Each yacht sends on one frequency and listens on another
o: Duplex channels are receive-only for small craft
Your squelch is set too high for a duplex channel
Duplex channels need both sets on high power
why: On duplex a ship sends on one frequency and receives the shore's; two ships cannot hear each other.

q: The coast station asks you to switch to its working channel, which is duplex. Can you talk to it there?
a: Yes — duplex works between a ship and a shore station
o: No — yachts may only use simplex channels
No — duplex works only between two ships
Only if you first send a DSC call on 70
why: Duplex channels are made for ship-to-shore calls; only ship-to-ship fails on them.

q: On channel 72 you and your friend press the transmit button at the same moment. What happens?
a: Neither hears the other — on simplex only one can transmit at a time
o: Both are heard, as in a telephone conversation
The set holds the second call until the first ends
The stronger signal is passed on to the other boat
why: Simplex is one frequency: while you transmit you cannot receive, so talk in turn and end with OVER.

q: You are approaching an island port in Greece and want the port authority's working channel. Where do you find it?
a: In the pilot book, almanac or port details on the chart
o: It is always channel 12 in every Greek port
It is always channel 70, as for all port calls
Ask any yacht on 72 which channel they think it is
why: Port channels differ from port to port; look them up rather than guess.

q: Your friend cannot hear you, although you are only 6 miles apart. Why?
a: VHF works roughly in line of sight, and the island is in the way
o: Six miles is beyond the range of any yacht VHF
The island's harbour channel jams the intership one
VHF bends around islands only on channel 16
why: VHF travels roughly in straight lines; high land between the antennas blocks it.

fig.note: A: you · B: your friend, 6 miles away

q: Which of these may stay on channel 16 instead of moving to another channel?
a: Distress traffic: a MAYDAY and the replies to it
o: A friendly chat between two yachts
Booking a berth with the marina
The coastguard's full weather forecast
why: 16 is for distress, urgency, safety and calling; only distress traffic normally stays on it.

q: You are approaching a busy commercial port where large ships manoeuvre. Which channel do you listen to as well as 16?
a: The port's own operations or traffic channel
o: Channel 70, to hear the ships' DSC alerts
Channel 72, where ships give way to yachts
No other channel — 16 is enough in a port
why: Near a busy port, listen on its listed port or traffic channel to know what ships will do.

q: On your charter yacht in Croatia, the VHF display shows "USA" next to the channel number. What do you do?
a: Set the channel mode to international (INT)
o: Leave it: channel modes only matter for DSC
Leave it: USA mode gives the longest range
Set the mode to CAN, as used in Europe
why: Outside North America use the international channel plan; some channels differ in USA mode.

q: You and your friend move to 72, but two other boats are already talking there. What do you do?
a: Agree another free intership channel, such as 77
o: Talk over them — 72 is open to everyone
Go back to 16 and have your chat there
Use channel 70, which is always free
why: Never talk over others; pick another free intership channel.

q: Your flotilla agreed this morning to keep a watch on 72 as well as 16. You want to reach the lead boat. Where do you call?
o: On 16 first, then move to 72
On 70, then talk on 72
On 6, then move to 72
why: A pre-arranged working channel can be used for the call itself, keeping 16 clear.

q: Which set of channels fits these three jobs, in order?
why: 13 bridge-to-bridge safety, 72 intership chat, 70 DSC only.

fig.title: Three jobs
lines: 1. Agree how to pass a ship that called you
2. A long chat with a friend's yacht
3. The channel your DSC uses for alerts

q: From A you talk easily to the coast station, but your friends at B cannot hear you. Why?
a: The coast station's antenna is very high; the headland blocks B
o: The coast station is on duplex, which carries further
Friends' sets need DSC to hear a yacht nearby
Short distances are weaker than long ones on VHF
why: Range depends on antenna height and a clear line; high stations reach far, land in between blocks.

labels: coast station on a mountain, 30 miles north
fig.note: A: you · B: your friends, 3 miles away

q: Channel 16 is busy with a long MAYDAY exchange between the coastguard and a yacht. You need to tell the marina you will be late. What do you do?
a: Call the marina directly on its working channel
o: Wait for a gap and call the marina on 16
Call the marina briefly on 16 at low power
Call the marina on 70, which stays free
why: Keep off 16 during distress traffic; routine calls go straight to the working channel.

q: Your three flotilla friends are at sea in these places. Both your boats have masthead antennas. Whom can you count on reaching by voice?
o: A and B
A and C
All three
why: Yacht to yacht reaches roughly 10–20 miles over open water; high land between blocks it.

lines: A: 8 miles away, open water between
B: 12 miles, behind a 400 m island
C: 40 miles away, open water between
